After eons of pressure to hasten the vulnerable metamorphosis that transforms a caterpillar into a butterfly, one species developed 
wing-like membranes during its larval form and simply continued feasting. Th is form of neoteny forced the creature to forgo the usual 
brief life span of sexual maturity and, instead the insect now grows large and lives past their year-long lifespan, hibernating in leafy 
nests and reaching egg laying adulthood once growing to a foot in length. While not capable of true flight like a butterfly, the drafi an, in 
its near larval state can nonetheless glide across great distances to fi nd rich feeding grounds. Such a gentle flight would be an easy meal 
for most predators had the drafi an’s bodily fluids not be suffused with a neurotoxin from feasting on the toxic leaves of a drafwood tree.

Encountering With little to concern itself besides eating and 
breeding, the drafi an is either evading or gliding across the 
Farplains in search of plants to feed on during the spring and 
summer months. Most predators stay clear of the bright green 
insect for the ill effects of its blood and potentially fatal strands 
of silk that stretch across the fi elds. 
Folding its wing-membranes close 
to its body, the drafian navigates 
along treetops in a similar manner 
to its larval caterpillar origins. When 
needing to move quickly, it launches 
itself upwards and spreads the thin 
jelly-like skin out to glide effortlessly
Rows of spiracles adorn the sides of the soft fleshed 
insect. These allow the creature to grow large as it 
can take in vast amounts of oxygen when in flight
Large eyes sit along the sides of its 
chitinous head. With keen vision, 
the drafian spies foliage on the far 
horizon allowing it to migrate across 
even the arid wastes of the Grayfynn
A wide sail-like membrane spreads 
outwards to catch updrafts and 
allow the drafian to glide effortlessly 
across fields and rivers
